text: July fourteenth, eighteen eighty-two. A teamster hauling wood up a mountain road in southeastern Arizona notices a man sitting against an oak tree, right beside the creek.
From a distance, he looks like he's resting. Two women had ridden past him the day before and thought exactly that.
He wasn't resting.

The man was Johnny Ringo, one of the most feared gunmen in the territory, an outlaw tied to the same feud that ended at the O K Corral. He had a revolver in his right hand and a single bullet wound in his head. His boots were gone. His feet were wrapped in strips torn from his own undershirt. His gun belt was buckled on upside down. And part of his scalp had been cut away.
The local jury called it suicide. Almost nobody who has studied the case since has been comfortable with that answer.

Those mountains hold more than one unsolved story. They were the homeland of the Chiricahua Apache. They sheltered outlaws, hid a warrior who escaped a prison train, and turned a blind woman into a legend. They were made by a volcano so violent it makes Mount Saint Helens look like a firecracker.
And two days ago, on October twentieth, twenty twenty-six, they became America's newest national park, the sixty-fourth, and the first new one in nearly six years.
This is Chiricahua.

Drive about a hundred and twenty miles east of Tucson and the desert does something strange. Out of grassland and mesquite rises a range of mountains covered in forest, and inside them, thousands of stone columns standing shoulder to shoulder, like an army frozen in place.

The Chiricahua Apache called this place the land of the standing-up rocks. The settlers who came later called it the Wonderland of Rocks. Even the name of the mountains is old, "Chiricahua" is usually traced to an Opata word for "wild turkey."

Walk into Echo Canyon and the trail squeezes between walls of stone so close together that hikers call one stretch "Wall Street." Climb to the Heart of Rocks and the pillars crowd around you, some tall and thin as chimneys, others stacked like coins, others shaped so much like animals that early visitors gave them names: Duck on a Rock. The Totem Pole. Big Balanced Rock.
But none of it was here by accident. It was built in a single, violent geological instant.

To understand how it got here, you have to go back about twenty-seven million years. In what is now the Chiricahua Mountains, a series of enormous eruptions tore open the ground at a place geologists call the Turkey Creek caldera, a collapsed volcanic crater roughly twelve miles across and about five thousand feet deep.

The biggest of those eruptions threw out more than a thousand times the material of the nineteen eighty eruption of Mount Saint Helens. Searing clouds of ash and gas raced across the land and buried more than twelve hundred square miles.
When the ash settled, it was so hot that it welded itself together into solid rock, a pale volcanic stone called rhyolite, in places more than sixteen hundred feet thick.

Then time went to work. As the rock cooled, it cracked into vertical joints. Water slipped into those cracks. In winter it froze and expanded, prying the rock apart a fraction of an inch at a time. For millions of years, rain, ice and wind carved along those lines, until what was left were pillars, spires and boulders balanced on impossibly thin necks.
Some of these balanced rocks weigh hundreds of tons and sit on bases that look like they could tip over in a strong wind. They've stood like that for longer than humans have existed.

And from the top of the park, on the horizon to the north, the mountains form a shape that many visitors see as a giant face lying on its back, looking at the sky. It's called Cochise Head, named for the man whose story begins our next chapter.
And his story starts with a misunderstanding, one that would cost hundreds of lives.

For centuries before any of this was a park, these mountains were home to the Chiricahua Apache, four related bands whose territory stretched across southeastern Arizona, southwestern New Mexico and northern Mexico. They called themselves Ndé, "the people." The National Park Service describes them as superb warriors who fiercely resisted colonization for more than three centuries.
In the mid-eighteen hundreds, the most powerful leader among them was a man named Cochise, of the Chokonen band, whose people lived around Apache Pass and the mountains to the west.

A quick note before we go on: there is no known photograph of Cochise. Images online labeled with his name show other people. So in this story, you'll see the land he knew, not a face we can't verify.

In January of eighteen sixty-one, raiders struck a ranch south of Fort Buchanan, drove off cattle, and kidnapped a twelve-year-old boy named Felix Ward. The Army assumed Cochise was responsible. The Park Service's own history of Chiricahua says the raid was likely the work of a different Apache group entirely.

A young lieutenant named George Bascom rode to Apache Pass with fifty-four soldiers and invited Cochise to talk. On February fourth, inside an Army tent, Bascom accused him of the kidnapping and announced that Cochise would be held until the boy was returned.
Cochise drew a knife, slashed through the side of the tent and escaped into the hills. Several members of his family, including his brother, were left behind as hostages.

What followed spiraled out of control. Cochise returned under a white flag to ask for his people back. Talks failed. Apaches seized hostages of their own. On February eighth, Cochise and hundreds of warriors attacked, and later killed their captives. Days later, on February nineteenth, soldiers hanged six Apache men near the pass, Cochise's brother among them.
Historians call it the Bascom Affair. It helped ignite more than a decade of war across the region.

In July eighteen sixty-two, Cochise and his father-in-law, the leader Mangas Coloradas, ambushed a Union column at Apache Pass. The warriors held the high ground, until the soldiers brought up mountain howitzers. One Apache fighter later put it plainly: they would have won, if the soldiers hadn't fired wagons at them.
Mangas Coloradas was later killed after entering negotiations, and Cochise became the leading figure of Chiricahua resistance.

Peace finally came in eighteen seventy-two, and it came through friendship. A scout and prospector named Tom Jeffords rode into Cochise's mountain stronghold, nearly alone, with General Oliver O Howard. Cochise made them wait for days. Then, after long talks, he agreed to peace in exchange for a reservation on his own homeland. Jeffords became the agent, by the Park Service's account, the only white man Cochise ever considered a friend.

Two years later, in June eighteen seventy-four, Cochise died, probably of cancer. That night, his warriors painted his body and carried him into the mountains, and laid him to rest in a place only they knew. Jeffords was one of the very few outsiders who knew where. He kept that secret until his own death forty years later.
The location has never been revealed, and it shouldn't be. Some places are meant to stay with the people they belong to.
But the peace Cochise made did not outlive him for long. And within twelve years, nearly every Chiricahua Apache would be on a train heading east, except for one man, who refused to stay on it.

After Cochise's death, the government abolished his reservation and ordered the Chiricahua moved to San Carlos, far to the north. Many refused. Over the next decade, small bands broke away again and again, the most famous led by a Bedonkohe warrior named Geronimo.

By the summer of eighteen eighty-six, Geronimo's free band was down to thirty-seven people: eighteen warriors, thirteen women and six children, chased by thousands of soldiers across two countries. In early September eighteen eighty-six, in Skeleton Canyon, just southeast of the Chiricahua Mountains, they surrendered. Geronimo is recorded as saying: "Once I moved about like the wind. Now I surrender to you, and that is all."

What happened next is one of the darkest chapters of the era. The Army didn't just send Geronimo's band into exile. It sent nearly every Chiricahua Apache, including the scouts who had served the Army and helped track Geronimo down. They were loaded onto trains as prisoners of war and sent to Florida.

They would not be free again for twenty-seven years. They were moved from Florida to Alabama, and then to Fort Sill in Oklahoma. By the mid-eighteen nineties, roughly half had died of disease. Geronimo himself died at Fort Sill in nineteen oh nine, still a prisoner.

And here's a connection most visitors never hear: during the Geronimo campaign, Buffalo Soldiers of the Tenth Cavalry camped inside what is now the park, in Bonita Canyon. Some of those soldiers later helped guard the prisoners on the train east. Before they left, they carved their names into stone and built a small monument to President James Garfield. Archaeologists are still studying the site.
Somewhere in Missouri, as one of those trains labored up a steep grade, a man named Massai jumped.

Massai had been an Army scout. He was on the train anyway. According to the story his family later told, he became convinced the prisoners were going to be killed, and he chose to run. Traveling at night, he made his way back across hundreds of miles of unfamiliar country to the mountains of the Southwest.

What we know about his life after that comes largely from his own family. He married a young Mescalero woman named Zanagoliche, and for many years they lived hidden in the mountains, raising children far from any reservation. Settlers blamed him for raids and thefts, some of which, historians now suspect, he never committed.

Around nineteen oh six, Massai was killed by a posse in New Mexico. His daughter, Alberta Begay, later shared the family's memories with historian Eve Ball. Her mother's words, near the end of her life, were simple: "Your father was not a murderer. He killed only to protect us."

Today the highest viewpoint you can drive to in the park is called Massai Point. Even the Park Service admits the name may rest on a mistaken settler story about a horse thief. The family that ran the nearby ranch asked that it be named for him anyway.
Stand there at sunset and you can see why anyone would fight to come back. The canyons drop away in every direction, and the valleys below turn gold.
But in the years Massai was hiding in the mountains, those same valleys were filling with a different kind of fugitive.

By the early eighteen eighties, the Apache wars were not the only violence in these mountains. Silver had been found across southeastern Arizona, and boomtowns appeared almost overnight, Tombstone to the west, and a rough camp on the eastern slope of the Chiricahuas called Galeyville.

Galeyville lasted barely two years. At its peak, a few hundred people lived there. Popular history remembers it as the hideout of the Cowboys, a loose gang of rustlers and gunmen led by figures like Curly Bill Brocius and Johnny Ringo, the same men locked in a feud with Wyatt Earp and his brothers.

One night in May eighteen eighty-one, a drunk Curly Bill picked a fight in Galeyville with a man named Jim Wallace. Wallace shot him through the cheek and neck. Curly Bill survived. A court called it self-defense.

Curly Bill's real ending is its own mystery. In March eighteen eighty-two, Wyatt Earp said he killed him with a shotgun in a gunfight at a spring in the Whetstone Mountains. Two Tombstone newspapers offered rewards, one thousand and two thousand dollars, for proof that Curly Bill was dead. Nobody ever collected. His grave has never been found.

As for Galeyville, the silver turned out to be poorer than anyone hoped. The smelter was hauled away, the post office closed in eighteen eighty-two, and the town emptied. Today nothing is left standing, just foundations and old mine tailings in the grass.

Just to the southeast lay Skeleton Canyon, a smuggling route to Mexico said to be named for the bones left along it. In eighteen seventy-nine and again in eighteen eighty-one, Cowboys ambushed Mexican travelers there. Out of those attacks grew a legend: a treasure of gold and silver supposedly buried somewhere in the canyon. Treasure hunters have searched for more than a century. Arizona Highways magazine once called the tale "faded and doubtful." People still look.
Which brings us back to the man under the oak.

In July eighteen eighty-two, Johnny Ringo had been drinking heavily for days. A deputy met him on the road carrying two bottles of whiskey. On the afternoon of July thirteenth, people at a nearby ranch heard a single shot. The next day, his body was found in West Turkey Creek valley, within sight of the road.

Here is what the record says. He was sitting against the tree. Revolver in his right hand, rifle nearby. Boots missing, feet wrapped in strips of his undershirt. Two cartridge belts, one of them on upside down. And part of his scalp gone, in the words of the Tombstone Epitaph, "as if cut out by a knife."
Eleven local men served as the coroner's jury. None had forensic training. They ruled it suicide, and the newspaper noted that Ringo had often spoken of taking his own life.
But the strange details never went away.
Wyatt Earp? The theory comes mostly from a memoir later exposed as unreliable, and Earp himself publicly denied it.
Doc Holliday, the version Hollywood loves? Court records place him in Colorado at the time.
"Buckskin" Frank Leslie? He was reportedly seen trailing Ringo, later boasted about the killing, and one man who accused him was soon shot dead by Leslie. But there's no proof.
A gambler known as "Johnny-Behind-the-Deuce"? A rumor, with a lot of reasons to doubt it.
One historian's educated guess is that something spooked Ringo's horse, that he was caught on foot, and that someone shot him and took a trophy. Others still believe the jury got it right.
Johnny Ringo was buried right where he was found, at the foot of that tree. The grave is still there, on private land. And the case is still open, in the only court that's left, the court of history.
Back in Bonita Canyon, the same canyon where the Buffalo Soldiers camped, a very different story was beginning.

Neil Erickson was a Swedish immigrant who had fought in the Geronimo campaigns as a cavalry sergeant, and who would later become the very first ranger of the Chiricahua National Forest. Emma Peterson, also from Sweden, had worked as a maid for an Army colonel. They met at Fort Bowie, married in eighteen eighty-seven, and claimed a homestead in Bonita Canyon. Neil later wrote that Emma had found the place and thought it was the most gorgeous spot she had ever seen.
Their daughter Lillian was born in eighteen eighty-eight at the Fort Bowie hospital.

As tourists began discovering the rock formations, Lillian and her sister began taking in guests. They named it Faraway Ranch. Lillian and her husband Ed Riggs built some of the first trails through the rocks, and lobbied hard to protect them. In nineteen twenty-four, President Calvin Coolidge proclaimed Chiricahua National Monument.

A decade later, in the depths of the Great Depression, a camp of young men from the Civilian Conservation Corps arrived. They built roads, trails, a tunnel, a fire lookout and the stone overlook at Massai Point. At one point, seventeen of them worked barefoot because their shoes hadn't arrived, until a telegram to a U S senator finally got them boots.
And through it all, Lillian kept the ranch running. She had struggled with her hearing since childhood. In nineteen forty-two she lost her sight. By the end of her life she was blind and nearly deaf.

She kept running Faraway Ranch anyway, managing guests, cattle and staff, for nearly three more decades. A magazine writer who stayed with her in the late nineteen fifties gave her the nickname that stuck: the Lady Boss of Faraway Ranch.
Her public face was famously cheerful. Her private diary, preserved by the Park Service, tells a harder story, of loneliness, worry and the weight of holding everything together.
She closed the guest ranch in nineteen seventy and died in nineteen seventy-seven. Today, Faraway Ranch is part of the park, and you can walk through the rooms where she lived.
People came to Faraway Ranch for the rocks. But the mountains around it hold something even rarer than stone, and some of it was only caught on camera a few years ago.

Chiricahua is what scientists call a sky island: a mountain range that rises out of the desert so high that it carries its own islands of forest. In a single drive, you climb from desert grassland through oak woodland into pine and fir.

Because it sits where the Rocky Mountains, the Sierra Madre of Mexico and two great deserts meet, species from very different worlds overlap here. Coatis, raccoon relatives from the tropics, roam the canyons. Around two hundred kinds of birds have been recorded, including the brilliant elegant trogon that birders travel across the country to see.

And sometimes, something rarer moves through the dark. In twenty sixteen, a government trail camera photographed a wild jaguar in a range just north of here. The next year, a conservation group released video of a jaguar in the Chiricahua Mountains, a cat that local students named Sombra, "shadow." The group says its spot pattern matched the twenty sixteen animal.
Jaguars once roamed the American Southwest. Today, a single wandering cat is enough to make headlines.

The mountains shelter smaller rarities too: the Chiricahua leopard frog, a threatened species that has vanished from most of the places it once lived, and pines and squirrels whose closest relatives live far to the south in Mexico. For many of them, these forested peaks are an island, and the desert all around is the sea.

These mountains also carry scars. In twenty eleven, the Horseshoe Two Fire burned more than two hundred twenty thousand acres of the range and touched every acre of the monument in some way. The forest is still recovering, a reminder that this landscape is still changing.

In March twenty twenty-six, the House passed the Chiricahua National Park Act. On September thirtieth the Senate approved it unanimously. On October twentieth, Chiricahua became the sixty-fourth national park in the United States.

The boundaries didn't change. The name did, and so did the attention. The law also requires the Park Service to protect traditional cultural and religious sites, to consult with tribes, and to guarantee access for tribal members, including temporary closures when a tribe asks for privacy. The Apache people who call this their homeland are still here, and their connection to these mountains never ended.
It's a quiet place. One campground. No lodge. An International Dark Sky Park, where the stars are as sharp as they were when Cochise looked up at them.
A volcano built it. Ice carved it. Warriors defended it, outlaws hid in it, a blind woman kept it, and a jaguar still walks through it.
Welcome to Chiricahua, America's newest national park, and one of its oldest stories.
